client: I've been really struggling since my grandma passed away last month. I sit down to work and suddenly all these memories of her flood in, and I just can't focus on anything. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help - the pain feels too deep.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're grieving your grandmother's passing, and it makes complete sense that these precious memories would surface when you're trying to focus. The pain does feel overwhelming right now, and I want you to know your feelings are valid and important to honor. What's one small way you might create space for both your grief and your daily tasks today?

client: I appreciate you saying that, but it's hard to imagine making space for grief when everything feels so heavy. Even small tasks like making coffee remind me of her, and then I just freeze up. I'm not sure how to "create space" when the sadness feels like it's everywhere.
therapist: It sounds like these waves of grief are coming at unexpected moments, making even daily routines feel overwhelming right now. The way you describe freezing up shows how deeply connected your grandmother was to so many parts of your life. Would it feel possible to acknowledge these moments by simply saying "I miss you" when a memory arises, rather than trying to push through or stop the feeling?

client: I don't know... saying "I miss you" out loud feels kind of silly when I'm just standing in the grocery aisle because I saw her favorite cookies. People would think I'm crazy. And honestly, trying to acknowledge the grief makes it hurt more in the moment - that's why I try to push through it.
therapist: way that honors your feelings while feeling manageable?

client: I guess I'm just not sure how to honor my feelings when they feel so overwhelming. When I try to acknowledge my anxiety, it just seems to grow bigger instead of feeling manageable. Part of me worries that if I really let myself feel it, I'll just get stuck there forever.
therapist: I hear your fear that fully acknowledging these feelings might make them consume you, and that's a very understandable concern when grief feels so powerful. What if we thought about honoring your feelings in small doses - maybe setting aside just 5 minutes to remember your grandmother, then gently shifting focus? How does that idea sit with you?

client: I don't know... setting aside just 5 minutes feels like it might make the grief worse when the time's up. Like opening a door I can't close again. I've been trying so hard to keep busy so I don't have to feel this pain at all.
therapist: I hear how protective that busyness has been for you - it makes sense you'd want to avoid reopening wounds that feel so raw. That fear of the floodgates opening is very real when we've been holding so much at bay. What would it feel like to try acknowledging just one small memory of her today, perhaps while in a safe, private space?

client:
I don't know... even thinking about remembering her makes my chest feel tight. What if I start crying and can't stop? I've kept myself together by staying busy for so long, and I'm scared of what might happen if I let myself feel it. 

But part of me does wonder if maybe just thinking about one small, happy memory would be okay. Like when we used to bake cookies together. That doesn't seem as scary as thinking about the bad stuff.
therapist: I hear both your fear of being overwhelmed and that small, hopeful part of you that's considering a gentle memory - that's such an important observation you've made. The cookie-baking memory sounds like a beautiful place to start, precisely because it carries some warmth along with the sadness. Would you be willing to try holding that memory lightly, like looking at a photograph for just a moment, and notice what happens in your body when you do?

client: I can try, but I'm scared it'll just make me feel worse. That memory is nice but it also reminds me how alone I feel now without my grandma. My chest gets tight just thinking about it.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel that tightness when remembering such a meaningful connection that's now changed - that physical response shows how real your love and loss are. Maybe we could approach this gently by having you recall the smell of those cookies first, rather than diving straight into the full memory? What do you notice in your body as you imagine that warm, comforting scent?

client:
I don't know... even the smell of those cookies makes my chest hurt now. It just reminds me that I'll never get to bake with her again. I can almost smell the cinnamon, but then this wave of sadness hits and I want to stop thinking about it completely. 

Part of me feels like avoiding these memories would be easier than sitting with this pain. Why would I want to keep feeling this way on purpose?
therapist: I hear how much this hurts - that longing for what can't be is one of grief's most painful parts. You're absolutely right that avoiding the pain seems easier in the moment, yet I wonder if pushing away these memories might also make you feel more alone with them over time. Could we try something different - maybe letting the cinnamon scent be there while also noticing something comforting in the present moment, like the weight of your feet on the floor?

client: I get what you're saying about not avoiding the pain, but it's just so overwhelming when I smell cinnamon and remember baking with my mom. The idea of trying to focus on my feet or something else at the same time... I don't know, it feels like that would cheapen the memory somehow. Like I'm not honoring her properly if I'm not fully immersed in the grief when it comes up.
therapist: You're touching on something really important - this tension between honoring your mom's memory and protecting yourself from being overwhelmed by grief. It makes complete sense that you'd worry about doing her memory justice when the connection was so meaningful. What if we thought about it not as diluting the memory, but as helping you stay present enough to truly experience it without being swept away? How does that land for you?

client: I like the idea of staying present with her memory instead of getting lost in grief, but I'm scared that if I don't feel the pain as intensely, it means I'm forgetting her. The guilt creeps in whenever I have a good day or don't think about her for a few hours. It's like my sadness is the only proof that she still matters to me.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're holding onto this belief that your pain equals love - that's such a common and understandable fear in grief. Your grandmother's importance in your life isn't measured by your suffering, but by all the ways she shaped who you are. What would it feel like to consider that honoring her could also include carrying forward the love and lessons she gave you, not just the pain of missing her?
